newsitem.title: CHINA: US 7th Fleet on first visit to Chinese Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: US 7th Fleet on first visit to Chinese Hong Kong.

text.p: The flagship of the United States Seventh Fleet steamed into Hong Kong on Monday and invited China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) to lunch.

The amphibious command ship, the USS Blue Ridge, is the first foreign warship to visit these newly Chinese territorial waters since Britain handed the former colony back to Beijing's sovereignty five weeks ago.
Sailing into the world's busiest harbour in the wake of the worst typhoon in 14 years, the Blue Ridge took up a high-profile berth at Ocean Terminal, normally used by cruise liners.

Seventh Fleet commander Vice-Admiral Bob Natter said the U.S. Navy would continue to make 60 to 70 port calls per year at Hong Kong for recreation and supplies, despite the territory's July 1 reunification with communist-ruled China.
The ships stock up on supplies and the sailors go ashore to visit Hong Kong's shopping malls and nightlife spots, bringing US$50 million a year into the local economy.
Seventh Fleet commanders planned to meet China's garrison chief in Hong Kong, Major-General Liu Zhenwu, Natter said in an interview on board the ship.
"We have scheduled an official call tomorrow to visit the PLA garrison commander. We anticipate entertaining them to lunch on board tomorrow as well. We look forward to that very much.
"I anticipate our relationship with the PLA with be the same as the relationship with this city...essentially business as usual...and every indication is that this will be the case.
"It bodes well for our relationship both with China and with Hong Kong and for the economy of this great city," he said.
He said the U.S. Navy would like to join in athletic and social events with the PLA in Hong Kong.

A spokesman said the U.S. sailors were not allowed to visit the nearby Portuguese-ruled of Macau because of recent triad gang violence there. The U.S. Navy was concerned its sailors might get caught up in the trouble, the spokesman said.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen agreed in April that U.S. warships would continue to visit Hong Kong after the sovereignty change. Until that deal, the future of the visits had been in doubt.
"We're making every effort to work with the Chinese government, it is absolutely appropriate to have cooperative engagement with China," Natter said.

He said U.S. Navy port calls to Hong Kong send a signal "that we're here, and that we're very interested in being good neighbours, and very interested in maintaining the stability of this region which has been enjoyed for the last 50 years".
"It's to China's benefit, as well as the other nations in this region, that we have stability here," Natter said.
He said he expected in the near future U.S. warships would visit other Chinese ports where none had sailed in the recent past. The ship made a historic port visit to Shanghai in 1989.
The Blue Ridge was berthed across the harbour opposite the PLA's garrison headquarters, still named the Prince of Wales Barracks, where China has taken over defence duties from British troops.
More than two decades ago, the same ship was evacuating the U.S. military from Vietnam after the rout inflicted by China-backed and Soviet-backed Vietnamese Communist forces.
Natter said procedures for port calls to Hong Kong had changed very little since the handover, but were "a little slower" than when the territory was under the British flag.
The conventionally powered Blue Ridge operates from Japan and makes regular calls to Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand and Australia. It carries up to 1,500 personnel.
